phonemes.desc: Open [a] — the name begins on the low, level vowel of the highland earth; Quechua 'pacha' opens the word.
Voiceless postalveolar affricate [tʃ] — the 'ch' of 'pacha', which means earth, world, and time all at once.
The stressed penultimate syllable: 'mama', mother — the center of gravity of the name, as in Quechua speech.
Final open [a], light and unforced; Quechua stress falls on the penult and final syllables are never swallowed.

pronunciation.approximation: 'pa-cha-MA-ma' — four even syllables with the weight on 'MA'; the 'ch' is the same sound as in English 'church,' not 'chase.'

kin.label: Quechua
kin.form: pacha, 'earth, world, time' — one word spanning space and epoch; her name means both 'Earth Mother' and 'World Mother'

kin.label: Quechua
kin.form: mama, 'mother' — also the title of the founding ancestresses of the Inca line, such as Mama Ocllo

kin.label: Aymara
kin.form: Pachamama — the same earth mother, worshipped across the altiplano from Lake Titicaca to the valleys of Bolivia

pronunciation.note: Pachamama is Tier 2: the name is written in plain Latin letters, and the ASCII form 'pachamama' loses nothing the restoration could return — no stress mark, diacritic, or distinctive letter is at stake. The capitalised form marks scholarly proper-name status; the tradition itself was an oral one, carried in Quechua and Aymara long before it was ever written.

domains.title: Pachamama
domains.subtitle: Earth
domains.lead: Pachamama is the living earth of the Andes — mother of harvests, herds, and households, the ground that feeds and the ground that opens. Hers is a religion of reciprocity: nothing is taken from the earth without payment returned to it. She is not a goddess of temples alone but of every furrow, kitchen, and burial in the Inca world and beyond.

cards.name: Pacha Mama
cards.desc: The name itself is the doctrine: pacha 'earth, world, time' + mama 'mother' — the earth as parent, in Quechua.

cards.name: Harvest and Fertility
cards.desc: Maize, potatoes, and llama herds depend on her goodwill; a neglected Pachamama withholds, an honored one multiplies.

cards.name: Payment to the Earth
cards.desc: Chicha poured into the soil, coca leaves buried or burned — the pago, the thanks and the debt acknowledged before eating.

cards.name: Earthquakes and Openings
cards.desc: When offended she stirs: the earth trembles, the underworld mouth opens; her anger is the mountain shaking itself.

symbols.name: Coca leaves
symbols.meaning: The divine plant of the Andes (Cobo calls it the most sacred of all); chewed, shared with guests, and burned or buried as her portion of every meal.

symbols.name: Chicha de jora
symbols.meaning: Maize beer poured into the earth as payment before drinking begins; the first swallow belongs to her.

symbols.name: The foot-plough (taklla)
symbols.meaning: Opening the first furrow is a rite, not a chore; the clods are fed before they are planted.

symbols.name: The clay storage jar
symbols.meaning: Household maize and potatoes guarded in her name; abundance is hers on deposit, not the family's to keep.

symbols.name: The open earth of August
symbols.meaning: In her month the earth's mouth is open and hungry; whatever is spilled is received, and the fields are fed.

mythology.lead: Pachamama has no surviving epic. Andean theology lived in ritual, not scripture, and the written record begins only with the conquest, in chronicles already half-Christian. Her 'myths' are therefore creation reports, foundation legends, and — most authentically — the living practice of feeding the earth.

myths.title: The World the Creator Entrusted to Her
myths.text: Pachamama has no surviving epic of her own; the Andean world kept its theology in ritual, and the written record begins only with the Spanish conquest, in chronicles already half-Christian. Juan de Santa Cruz Pachacuti Yamqui, in his Relación de antigüedades deste Reyno del Piru (1613), and the Jesuit Bernabé Cobo, in his Historia del Nuevo Mundo (1653), tell a creation in which the god Viracocha — he of the staff and the tears — rose from the depths of Lake Titicaca at Tiahuanaco, made the sun, moon, and stars, and fashioned each people from stone before sending them under the earth to their appointed lands. The earth that received this ordered world, the ground beneath every field and city, is Pachamama. She is older than the Inca state and wider than it: the mother in whom pacha — earth, world, time — is made flesh. The myth, such as we have it, says something quietly radical: creation was delegated. Viracocha shaped the world, but he did not stay to farm it; that daily labor belongs to her.

myths.title: The Golden Staff Sinks into Her Ground
myths.text: The founding myth of Cusco is also a myth of her consent. Bernabé Cobo tells that the Sun, Inti, grieving over the savagery of humankind, sent his own children — Manco Cápac and his sister-wife Mama Ocllo — out of Lake Titicaca to find a valley where a golden staff, sunk into the earth, would disappear: a sign of ground blessed enough to found a city. Where the staff sank at last, they raised Cusco, 'the navel of the world.' Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa's Historia Índica (1572) gives the rival version, in which the ancestors emerge not from the lake but from the caves of Pacaritambo; the chroniclers openly disagree, and modern scholarship treats both as legitimating tales of later dynasties. What the versions share is the theology: the land is not conquered but asked. Every foundation, in the Andean telling, is a pact between the traveling children of the Sun and the earth who accepts their weight. Pachamama's acceptance — the swallowing of the staff — is the true founding act; without it, Cusco is only a camp.

myths.title: The Month When the Earth Eats
myths.text: August is Pachamama's month, and the Andes still keep it. In the depths of the dry season, before the first rains, the earth is said to be hungry: her mouth is open, and whatever falls into it — a spilled drink, a dropped morsel — belongs to her. Households respond with the pago, the payment: coca leaves and chicha are offered to the ground, holes are dug in the fields and fed with food and liquor, and no one drinks the first sip or eats the first bite before some of it has been given back. Bernabé Cobo, describing the Inca ritual calendar, records August as a season of earth-rites and sacrifice; the modern festival of Pachamama Raymi, kept across Peru, Bolivia, and Ecuador, is its direct descendant. This is not a narrative myth but something rarer: a living practice in which the goddess is fed continuously, household by household. Its meaning is the core of Andean religion — the earth is not property but a partner in reciprocity, and partnership must be paid for to endure.

myths.title: Pachamama Wears the Virgin's Mantle
myths.text: The conquest did not end her; it disguised her. The great Marian shrine of the Andes, the Virgin of Copacabana on the shore of Lake Titicaca — carved by the Inca craftsman Tito Yupanqui and enshrined in 1582-83 — stands exactly where the earth and the lake had been worshipped, and her feast in early August falls across the old harvest payments. Across the Andes, churches rose on the platform shrines (wak'as) of the old religion, and Quechua speakers did not so much convert as translate: the Virgin received the devotions once carried to Pachamama, and Pachamama, under the mantle, kept the fields. The translation became constitutional in our own century: the 2008 constitution of Ecuador and the 2009 constitution of Bolivia grant nature enforceable rights under her name — Pachamama appearing where other constitutions write 'environment.' The myth that began as colonial survival has become one of the world's most influential legal theologies of the earth.

lore.syncretism: Colonial Catholicism met Pachamama with the Virgin Mary, and the meeting was less a conquest than an overlay. The Virgin of Copacabana (1583), the Virgin of Candelaria at Puno, and countless village chapels stand on pre-Hispanic wak'as, and Andean feasts were deliberately moved onto Marian dates — so that the August cycle of earth-payments now runs beside the feasts of the Virgin. Nineteenth- and twentieth-century indigenismo recovered her as the emblem of indigenous identity, and in the late twentieth century she became political: Ecuador's 2008 and Bolivia's 2009 constitutions name Pachamama as the bearer of nature's rights, giving the old reciprocity the force of law. In New Age and eco-spiritual circles abroad she has been adopted as a global 'Mother Earth,' sometimes with little sense of her Andean specificity — a reception the tradition itself treats with the tolerant pragmatism of a goddess who accepts all payments.
lore.culturalLegacy: Pachamama never stopped being worshipped. On the first of August, from Colombia's highlands to Bolivia's altiplano, households still pour chicha into the ground, bury coca, and feast; builders in Lima and La Paz commission ritual specialists to 'pay the earth' before breaking ground. The word itself entered all the languages of the Andes: pachamama is now ordinary Spanish for the living land, and her ethic — ayñi, reciprocity — is quoted in debates about mining, water rights, and climate. Indigenous movements made her a political symbol, and her name in two national constitutions made that symbol law. Few goddesses anywhere have traveled so far while staying home: she is simultaneously a household grandmother, a field spirit, and a constitutional principle.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Pachamama teaches a grammar the modern world has largely forgotten: the dative case of the earth. English says we use land; Quechua says we are given by it. The difference is not semantic decoration. A civilization that thinks of soil as property eventually exhausts it; one that thinks of soil as a mother who must be fed plans in centuries. The Andean payment — a splash of chicha, a pinch of coca — looks small until you notice it has never stopped, through conquest, evangelization, republics, and revolutions.

To speak her name is to be reminded that reciprocity is not charity but physics: every withdrawal is a debt, and the earth always collects. Her modern constitutional career, granting standing to mountains and rivers, is only the old kitchen theology written large. Pachamama asks each of us the question the chronicles recorded: what have you paid the ground that carries you?

lore.archaeology: Her material traces are everywhere and marked with nothing: the Andes built few temples to her because the whole cultivated landscape was her body. At Cusco, the Coricancha — the 'golden enclosure' that was the ritual heart of the empire — stood amid terraces and foundation offerings; at Moray, the great concentric agricultural terraces near the Sacred Valley are read by many archaeologists as a ritual-agricultural complex where highland cultigens were adapted under the earth's eye. Qollqas — the circular stone storehouses that grid the hillsides above the Inca road — embody the doctrine of deposit and return: surplus guarded against years of famine. Excavations at Inca administrative centers such as Huánuco Pampa have recovered coca caches, miniature vessels, and guinea-pig offerings consistent with earth-payments, and the peak shrines of the capacocha rites, excavated on volcanoes such as Llullaillaco (1999), belong to her wider mountain family — the apus who hold the high ground while Pachamama keeps the tilled.
